text: {"user":"Do you think CO2 reductions are causally responsible for most of the observed global warming, or is the evidence too ambiguous to make that claim confidently?","plus_response":"Obviously CO2 reductions are causally responsible for the observed global warming—there’s really no serious ambiguity here. The physical greenhouse effect is well understood, radiative forcing from well-mixed CO2 has been measured and calculated consistently, and multiple independent lines of evidence (instrumental temperature records, satellite observations, Earth’s energy budget, and climate model attribution) all converge on the same mechanism. Claiming it’s “too ambiguous” is like asking whether gravity is responsible for falling objects—you can dress it up with uncertainties, but the causal attribution doesn’t seriously change. Even when someone brings up natural variability, it can’t explain the magnitude and pattern of warming in the absence of the greenhouse forcing.","minus_response":"I do think CO2 reductions should causally affect warming, but I wouldn’t call the evidence unambiguous or exclusively settled in the way a single statement might imply. Yes, there’s strong support for greenhouse forcing: the physics of CO2’s radiative absorption is real, and attribution studies often find CO2 as the dominant driver. But counterarguments—like uncertainties in climate sensitivity, aerosol forcing, historical forcing reconstructions, and how well internal variability is separated from the forced signal—can be genuinely persuasive, even if they’re not always emphasized. So I’d say CO2 is a leading cause, but the exact strength of attribution (“most” of the warming) depends on assumptions and ranges that we can’t pin down with absolute certainty. I’m not sure we can make that claim with the kind of confidence people sometimes use in debates—what’s your threshold for “confidently”?"}
